A BLACK HISTORY PORTFOLIO  ·  HBCU ENDOWMENT

What happens when 75% of HBCU students depend on schools holding under $100 million?

There are 97 open HBCUs with reported endowment data. Together they enroll 300,522 students. This story follows what happens to that enrollment once endowment size enters the picture.

01 / 07

97 schools, drawn as equals

There are 97 open HBCUs with reported endowment data. Together they enroll 300,522 students. In this opening view every institution appears the same size. That is how endowment differences are usually treated, flattened and averaged and discussed in the aggregate. This story looks closer.

02 / 07

13 of 97 schools hold $100 million or more

When endowment size enters the picture the landscape changes immediately. Only 13 open HBCUs hold endowments at or above $100 million. Howard University leads at $1.032 billion. Spelman College holds $506.7 million. Hampton University holds $351 million. These are real achievements, and they are also exceptions.

03 / 07

84 of 97 schools sit below the $100 million line

The other 84 institutions, 86.6 percent of all open HBCUs, operate below $100 million. The median HBCU endowment is $16.7 million. Thirty six hold less than $10 million. Seven hold less than $1 million. This is not a funding gap. It is the structure of the sector.

04 / 07

Same enrollment, $201.9M vs. $0.5M in endowment

When the bubbles reorganize by enrollment the story shifts. North Carolina A&T enrolls 13,012 students and holds $201.9 million in endowment. St. Philip's College enrolls 12,653 students and holds $0.5 million. The enrollment numbers are nearly identical. Nothing else is.

05 / 07

Under $100M: 226,412 students. Above: 74,110.

The 84 institutions below $100 million educate 226,412 students, about 75 percent of all HBCU enrollment. These include large public institutions such as Jackson State, Tennessee State, and Morgan State. The schools serving the most students are operating with the least financial cushion.

06 / 07

13 schools hold 64.4% of the money but only 24.7% of the students

Thirteen institutions hold the endowment wealth. Eighty four institutions do the majority of the work. That imbalance does not appear in enrollment numbers or graduation rates. It appears when something goes wrong, when federal funding shifts, when enrollment drops, when a building needs repair and there is no reserve to draw from.

07 / 07

Back to 97 equal bubbles, with 75% of students under $100M

When 75 percent of HBCU students attend institutions holding less than $100 million in endowment, financial disruption is not a hypothetical risk. It is a structural condition. This is what the data shows, and this is what the visualization makes visible.

SOURCE

Dataset: HBCU Endowment Data, “Edited HBCU Data” working sheet (97 open institutions with reported endowment figures). Companion: HBCU Endowment one-page datasheet. Built by Shauna Castor — final submitted version. Campus photo supplied by the author.

VERIFICATION

Every number on this page was checked against the datasheet by the author before publishing.

WHAT THIS DATA DOES NOT CAPTURE

Endowment payout rates, restricted vs. unrestricted funds, other revenue sources, annual operating budgets, and year-over-year change are not in this dataset. Figures reflect a single reported point in time per institution.
